title: The SPAN Story
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
In policy meetings, the chairs are always counted, but youth voices rarely are. That’s what sparked the founding of SPAN, Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide, in March 2025, what began as a handful of students has grown into a national youth-led coalition with real legislative impact. In just a few months, SPAN has helped shape 15 pieces of healthcare legislation across four states, proving that student voices don’t just belong in the conversation; they move it forward.

SPAN is a student-powered policy organization working to make healthcare more patient-centered, equitable, and accessible. We train high school and college students to write policy memos, deliver public testimony, and meet with lawmakers. Our students fight for reforms that directly affect their communities — from expanding mental health access in schools to increasing transparency in hospitals. Our initiatives are entirely youth-run, supported by a national team that provides legal, legislative, and research support to help students turn their ideas into action.

At SPAN, we don’t treat advocacy as a future goal. We treat it as a responsibility now. At SPAN, we don’t wait to be given influence. We earn it. Through research, advocacy, and action, our students are stepping into policy spaces and leaving a mark.

Because when young people are not just present but heard, we don’t just count the chairs in the room: we reshape the room entirely.

Learn more at spanationwide.org.

  • Written by Ashita Virani, Editorial & Business Lead at SPAN.

title: AI in Healthcare: Transforming Diagnosis, Documentation, and Patient Monitoring
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
Artificial Intelligence

Healthcare

Diagnosis

Patients

Advocacy

When a patient walks into a clinic today, the first observer might not be a doctor. It could be an algorithm. Artificial intelligence (AI) has quietly become the unseen assistant in hospitals and clinics around the world, helping physicians diagnose diseases, document visits, and monitor patients with a level of precision once thought impossible. What was once an ambitious idea at the intersection of technology and medicine is now an integral part of modern care.

AI in Diagnosis

AI’s most visible impact lies in diagnosis. Machine learning models trained on thousands of medical images can now detect conditions ranging from cancer to pneumonia with remarkable accuracy. Tools such as Google’s DeepMind and Aidoc help radiologists interpret scans faster, flagging subtle abnormalities that may escape even trained eyes. In dermatology, AI can distinguish between benign and malignant skin lesions in seconds, while in cardiology, predictive models assess the risk of heart disease long before symptoms appear.

These systems do not replace human judgment; they refine it. By handling repetitive analysis and providing data-driven insights, AI allows clinicians to focus on empathy, interpretation, and treatment, reinforcing the human core of healthcare rather than removing it.

AI in Documentation

Beyond diagnosis, AI is transforming the less glamorous but equally essential realm of medical documentation. Tools like Nuance’s Dragon Medical One and Suki AI use natural language processing (NLP) to transcribe and organize physician-patient conversations into detailed medical notes. This automation reduces the hours physicians spend typing, minimizing burnout and freeing up time for patient care.

AI in Patient Monitoring

Perhaps the most personal role of AI appears in patient monitoring. Wearable devices powered by AI track vital signs such as heart rate, oxygen levels, and sleep cycles, creating a continuous stream of data that physicians can interpret remotely. Systems like Biofourmis and Current Health even predict medical emergencies such as sepsis or heart failure before they occur, prompting earlier intervention.

This predictive monitoring represents a profound shift from reactive medicine to proactive prevention. For patients with chronic illnesses, AI does not just observe. It listens, learns, and alerts, providing reassurance that help is available before crisis strikes.

Challenges and Ethics

Still, the path forward demands caution. AI models can inherit biases from their data, raising ethical concerns about fairness and accuracy. Privacy, transparency, and accountability must remain central to AI development. The challenge is not only to create smarter algorithms but also to build trust between humans and machines, ensuring technology complements compassion rather than competes with it.

Conclusion

When a patient walks into a clinic tomorrow, AI will again be there, analyzing, documenting, and monitoring with quiet precision. Yet the true promise of this technology is not in replacing the doctor’s intuition; it is in amplifying it. AI’s strength lies in partnership, not supremacy. As healthcare continues to evolve, the goal remains unchanged: to heal with both intelligence and humanity. In this full circle, AI becomes what it was always meant to be, not a machine that replaces care but one that helps us care better.

  • Written by Ashita Virani, Editorial & Business Lead at SPAN.

title: Do Physician-Owned Hospitals Deserve a Second Look?
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
Physician-owned hospitals (POHs) have sparked a long-standing debate about the balance of cost, quality, and ethics of POHs within the U.S. healthcare system. Supporters of POHs argue that physician ownership encourages innovation, efficiency, higher-quality, and more patient-centered care. On the other hand, critics of POHs highlight the possibility for scrupulous business practices, such as self-referral, overutilization, and selective treatment of healthier, more profitable patients, also known as cherry-picking. These concerns led to calls for federal intervention, most notably the Affordable Care Act’s restrictions on POHs, which prevented their expansion despite the fact that multiple studies supporting that they deliver equal or superior cost efficiency and care quality. As healthcare policymakers continue to search for methods to improve the industry without sacrificing equality to cherry-picking or ease of access to all patients. As healthcare policymakers continue to search for methods to improve the industry without sacrificing equality to cherry-picking or ease of access to all patients, the controversy surrounding POHs patient benefits and discrimination raises a crucial question: should POHs remain under strict legislative restrictions, or should modern policymakers re-evaluate the role of POHs within the healthcare system?

History

Concerns about physician self-referral and conflicts of interest, particularly that physician ownership might lead to overuse, “cherry picking” of healthier patients with better insurance, and leave community hospitals with sicker, unprofitable patients, led Congress to gradually limit the number of physician-owned hospitals in a series of legislation culminating in Section 6001 of the Affordable Care Act (2010), which effectively prohibited the construction of new POHs and significantly curbed any further growth of existing ones as a condition of Medicare program participation. These restrictions built on earlier efforts like the Stark Law and the 2003 Medicare moratorium, reflecting long-standing fears that financial incentives could distort clinical decision-making and threaten the financial stability of full-service community and rural hospitals. However, in the years since, studies and policy evaluations, such as those related to the Ways & Means-associated manuscript, have raised doubts about the content of such concerns, noting that POHs appear to provide equivalent, if not better, quality of care at significantly lower cost to Medicare. Consequently, future policy has increasingly turned to an easing of restrictions imposed by ACA legislation, particularly in rural regions, while still proposing allowance for the growth of POHs, though under a watchful eye, to ensure that no potentially questionable ethics are involved.

Benefits

POHs have been shown in multiple cases to offer substantial cost savings when it comes to Medicare, particularly for especially expensive visits. A paper by UConn Health and Loyola University Chicago found that POHs could save Medicare over $1.1 billion annually on the total cost of care across 20 of the most expensive conditions, with cost reductions ranging from 8.6% to 15.2% compared with other hospitals in the same region. Critics would argue that these cost benefits could have come from cherry-picking healthier patients who are more profitable, but researchers found that patients treated at POHs had similar demographic and health history profiles. These researchers went on to mention that physician ownership often leads to better aligned management that keeps clinical decision-making in mind, reducing unnecessary utilization, streamlining care paths, and promoting a more efficient use of hospital resources. By promoting accountability and focusing on value-driven care, well-structured POHs can contribute to a more cost-effective healthcare system without sacrificing quality, access, or fairness in patient treatment, cementing them as a major resource for creating a better healthcare system.

Risks

However, some analyses from organizations like the American Hospital Association emphasize risks associated with expanding POHs, particularly in rural and underserved areas. In these areas, hospitals focused on comprehensive care and available 24/7 are crucial as these hospitals may be the only ones for miles. Studies have repeatedly found that some POHs tend to focus on a narrower range of specialized services, treat a healthier, commercially insured patient mix, and provide fewer emergency and high-acuity services than full-service community hospitals, which can shift costly emergency care burdens onto other providers, and in the worst case, make emergency care inaccessible due to transport time and overcapacity. Moreover, modeling analyses suggest that the entrance of a POH into the same market as a sole community hospital could significantly reduce the community hospital’s financial margins, potentially jeopardizing its ability to sustain essential services, retain staff, and remain open; this competition may appear to encourage higher quality care, but in reality, it often drains resources and puts unnecessary stress on an already high-tension environment. These concerns underscore the importance of crafting policy that preserves access while exploring the cost-efficiency benefits POHs may offer.

Conclusion

Overall, the debate concerning POHs is an argument about ethics and efficiency. Although concerns about encroaching on pre-existing hospitals, self-referral, and cherry-picking greatly warrant oversight, there is plenty of evidence to suggest that POHs can deliver high-quality care at lower cost, especially for common and expensive conditions, without compromising quality of care. Instead of broad restrictions out of fear-mongering, policymakers should pursue a more balanced approach that allows carefully regulated POHs to operate alongside community hospitals, with specific legislation to protect emergency access and scarce rural areas. In a modern-day America that values high-quality care along with reducing the heavily taxing cost of healthcare, physician-owned hospitals do not represent a threat to the healthcare system, but a potential solution to improve efficiency, accountability, and patient-centered care when watched carefully.

  • Written by Nicholas Wright, Content Editor-in-Chief at SPAN.

title: The GLP-1 Drug Revolution
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
One of the main spectacles of the Super Bowl is its commercials. While watching Super Bowl LX, hoping to see creative and humorous advertisements, I instead saw two commercials for Wegovy and Zepbound. Both commercials emphasized a single selling point: weight loss. Both companies are the main new competitors in the space of a revolutionary drug, GLP-1. This type of drug, GLP-1, is not a new thing; Ozempic has been around since 2017, but these drugs were initially advertised for type II diabetes, but have now since been used by celebrities and others for cosmetic weight loss. Although these drugs do help with weight loss, the other health benefits they provide should be what they focus on more, and the cost of these drugs are increasing due to the advertisement as a drug that can be used by anybody. These factors contribute to a GLP-1 revolution, but in the wrong direction.

Background

GLP-1 drugs (or agonists) are drugs that operate by mimicking the GLP-1 hormone, which is produced by the small intestine. It triggers insulin release, blocks glucagon secretion, and affects the part of the brain that makes you feel “full.” The first agonist to be approved by the FDA was in 2005, and since then many different companies have their own for different purposes.

Support

These drugs provide extraordinary gastro-intestinal health benefits, but they are not limited to just that. GLP-1 drugs have been prescribed for heart disease prevention, lowering blood pressure, and improving fatty liver disease. These other health benefits, along with the initial prescription for diabetes and blood sugar regulation, are deserving enough for GLP-1 drugs to be widely available to the public. Weight loss and the fight against obesity are also worthy problems these drugs attempt to battle, and they are effective. These benefits along with evidence of improved behavioral and metabolic changes, make it clear that the emergence of these drugs are beneficial to patients and clinicians due to their versatility and effectiveness.

Critiques

One of the main issues with GLP-1 drugs are some of the side effects, where even low doses causes extreme nausea, and extreme cases see malnutrition due to the loss of appetite and vomiting, though these are issues you can see with any drug. The main issue with these drugs is the companies that hold them. The advertising, and pricing of these drugs is where the issues lie. The high premiums, wide variety of patient coverage, and effective monopolist companies cause the high pricing which makes these beneficial drugs nearly impossible to afford for lower income and poorly insured individuals. The more pressing concern lies not in the pharmacology of the drugs, but in their commercialization. Aggressive advertising campaigns increasingly target broad audiences seeking weight loss, regardless of medical necessity. This messaging risks framing GLP-1 drugs as lifestyle enhancers rather than serious medical treatments. There have also been non FDA approved GLP-1 compounds advertised online, which poses a risk for people who want to use these drugs but cannot afford them, and thus leading to a search for alternatives. Further transparency is needed in the advertising to educate the general public on who truly needs these medicines, as well as the other health benefits they can provide. The pricing issues can only really be addressed by insurance companies themselves, by making coverage for these drugs better and cost less for the plans that these coverages are included in.

Conclusion

GLP-1 drugs represent a breakthrough in metabolic medicine. Their ability to treat diabetes, reduce cardiovascular risk, and combat obesity makes them revolutionary. However, the current cultural and commercial focus on cosmetic weight loss risks distorting their purpose and limiting equitable access. If the GLP-1 revolution continues to prioritize marketing over medical necessity, it may ultimately undermine the very patients these drugs were designed to help. A shift toward responsible advertising, improved insurance coverage, and better public education would ensure that this pharmaceutical advancement moves in the right direction.

  • Written by Noah Love, Content Writer at SPAN.

content:
SPAN in Philadelphia: Civic Learning Week 2026

Earlier this month, I had the honor of attending the Civic Learning Week National Forum in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, representing Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide across two full days of conversation, panels, and ideas (March 9–10). Getting there was its own adventure: a delayed flight, a lot of airport waiting, and a few energy drinks in my system. But when I finally checked into the hotel and found myself ordering Belgian waffles delivered straight to my room, I figured the universe was balancing things out.

Jokes aside, what stays with me most from the trip isn’t the hotel: it’s what the experience confirmed about why SPAN exists in the first place.

When we secured our win on Texas HB 5294, mobilizing close to a hundred medical students to deliver letters, emails, phone calls, and in-person testimony in Austin, something became clear to me: there was no existing model for sustained youth engagement in the healthcare legislative process. Students were passionate, but the infrastructure to channel their energy into meaningful advocacy simply wasn’t there.

The stakes couldn’t be higher. Research from Stanford shows that democratic participation shapes health outcomes, not just politically, but materially. When people are engaged in the decisions that govern their healthcare, those decisions get better. And by extension, the people who will live the longest under any given decision should have a meaningful voice in crafting it. That means young people. I firmly believe that when students have a real seat at the table, their healthcare will directly improve as a result.

At the Forum, I had the privilege of sitting on a panel called “Student Perspectives on Liberty and Learning” alongside three exceptionally talented high school students. One of the themes I spoke to was a shift from partisan advocacy to issue-specific advocacy. At SPAN, we are intentionally nonpartisan; our Policy Analysts come to us with the issues that matter to them, not ones handed down through a political lens.

Skip to 11:43 to see me.

This distinction matters. It is what makes our advocacy authentic and what keeps students of all backgrounds, beliefs, and experiences at the center of the work.

The other idea I kept returning to on the panel was America at 250. I feel proud to take a step back to appreciate how far America has come: the abolition of slavery, women’s suffrage, worker protections, student rights. These were hard-won expansions of democratic access. But I think the next 250 years have to be about agency. Too often, we have the rights without the tools, the platforms, or the confidence to use them.

We exist precisely to close that gap. To give students not just a voice, but the skills and infrastructure to make that voice count.

I left Philly quite tired. I will say, however: there’s a lot in store for SPAN. Stay tuned.

– Written by Ben Kurian, Co-Founder & Director at SPAN.

Healing or Harvesting: The Case for Regulating Private Equity in Primary Care

Introduction

In an era of disappearing family practices and months-long waits for routine appointments, primary care in the United States is already under strain from burnout, low reimbursement, and staffing shortages. As private equity firms and corporate investors move into this vacuum, the future of medicine is being shaped as much by financial strategy as by patient need. This raises an increasingly urgent question: who owns your doctor? Primary care is one of the most important parts of the healthcare system. It is often the first point of contact for patients, plays a central role in preventive care, serves as the main setting for chronic disease management, and provides continuity of care over time. Yet primary care is struggling to remain sustainable, and private equity has begun stepping in as a possible source of support. Primary care in the United States is under growing strain from physician shortages, weak reimbursement, and administrative burden. While private equity has often been criticized for accelerating the corporatization of medicine, its role in primary care is more complicated. With proper oversight and regulation, private investment could help stabilize struggling practices rather than simply exploit them.

Background

Primary Care is one of the most important pieces of a country’s healthcare system, and it has been proven to have better population health, health equity, and healthcare quality for systems that focus on primary care. Primary care in the United States has been weakening for years due to a combination of low reimbursement, physician shortages, administrative burden, and burnout. Although primary care is often described as the foundation of the healthcare system, it is reimbursed less generously than procedural specialties and expected to manage an increasingly complex patient population with limited time and support. Independent practices have struggled to survive rising overhead costs, insurance complexity, and electronic documentation demands, leading many physicians to sell to larger systems or leave practice altogether. By the time private equity firms began moving into primary care more aggressively, they were entering a field that had already been destabilized by long-term structural neglect. This is a real issue, as we are seeing statistics showing that the share of physicians employed by hospitals or in practices at least partially owned by hospitals or health systems rose from 29% in 2012 to 41% in 2022.

Support

As primary care has become more financially vulnerable, private equity has stepped in. One reason primary care is attractive to investors is that it is a highly fragmented market made up of many small practices, creating opportunities for consolidation. There is also relatively predictable patient demand based on the population and geography surrounding a practice. In addition, investors may see opportunities to improve billing efficiency and increase profitability. The private equity model generally works by acquiring struggling or mid-sized practices and merging them into larger networks. After doing so, investors attempt to reduce costs, streamline operations, and increase profits before eventually selling the network for a return.

This model can offer some meaningful advantages for primary care. Investment is not inherently harmful, and primary care often needs capital that small independent practices cannot access on their own. Outside investment can help practices afford updated technology, hire additional staff, improve infrastructure, and remain open in communities with limited access to care. Private equity can also contribute to greater operational efficiency, expanded access to telehealth and data systems, and improved financial stability. In underserved areas especially, these investments may help preserve care that might otherwise disappear. For these reasons, private equity should not automatically be dismissed as incompatible with primary care. Under the right conditions, it may offer one possible path toward strengthening a struggling system.

These advantages make the potential investment of private equity an option to consider for a way to resurrect the Primary Care system.

Criticism

Despite these possible advantages, private equity brings serious risks because its primary goal is profit. A profit-first model can worsen many of the problems primary care already faces. Practices may be pressured to prioritize revenue over patient relationships, creating incentives for shorter visits, higher patient volumes, and greater emphasis on profitable services rather than comprehensive care. The FTC has already shown concern about private equity, and in this environment, the core values of primary care can become secondary to financial performance.

Private equity ownership can also reduce physician autonomy. When investors take control of a practice, physicians may have less authority over staffing, scheduling, and treatment flow. Clinical decisions can become increasingly shaped by business targets rather than solely by patient needs. This is especially concerning in primary care, where physicians must often manage complex and long-term conditions that require time, trust, and flexibility.

Another major concern is the threat to continuity of care. One of primary care’s greatest strengths is the long-term relationship between doctor and patient. However, consolidation and investor-driven management may lead to more rotating providers, a more retail-style approach to medicine, and weaker long-term doctor-patient connections. Consolidation also poses broader market risks. As practices merge and competition declines, prices can rise and smaller communities may lose independent healthcare options altogether. These risks make it necessary to view private equity not simply as a helpful source of capital, but as a powerful force that can reshape primary care in ways that may ultimately undermine its purpose.

Discussion

It is clear that primary care is in need of support, and investment alone is not inherently harmful. However, because private equity is fundamentally profit-oriented, an important question remains: how can it help more than it harms? The answer lies in regulation. Without meaningful oversight, investors are free to prioritize short-term profits with little regard for the patients and physicians whose work generates that profit. With effective regulation, however, private equity could be directed toward strengthening practices rather than exploiting them.

Such regulation could take several forms. Ownership transparency requirements would allow patients, physicians, and regulators to know who controls medical practices and how those financial relationships shape care. Restrictions on debt-loading acquired practices would help prevent investors from placing excessive financial burdens on the clinics they purchase. Quality-of-care benchmarks could ensure that profitability is not pursued at the expense of patient outcomes.

Some of the most important forms of regulation would include stronger antitrust review, where the FTC has already shown pushes in this area; FTC staff noted in 2024 that Indiana broadened its attorney general’s authority to monitor healthcare mergers and acquisitions, with the expanded oversight taking effect in July 2024. The other forms include protections for physician decision-making, and reimbursement structures tied more closely to outcomes than to volume. These reforms matter because the greatest risks of private equity are loss of autonomy, market consolidation, and high-volume profit-seeking. If revenue is tied instead to the quality of care delivered, private investment would have a stronger incentive to improve primary care rather than simply keeping it afloat long enough to produce returns. Regulation, then, is the most effective way to balance the financial goals of private equity with the broader public need for a strong and sustainable primary care system in the United States.

Conclusion

Primary care is one of the most essential parts of the American healthcare system, yet it has been weakened by years of physician shortages, low reimbursement, administrative burden, and structural underinvestment. In that weakened state, it has become vulnerable to outside ownership and financial consolidation. Private equity has entered primary care because the system is fragile, fragmented, and in need of capital. While this investment can provide financial support, technological modernization, and operational efficiency, it also carries significant risks to physician autonomy, continuity of care, and patient-centered medicine.

For that reason, the debate over private equity in primary care should not be framed as a simple choice between rejecting investment and accepting exploitation. The more important question is how investment is governed. With strong oversight, transparency, and quality-focused regulation, private equity could serve as a stabilizing force for practices that might otherwise close. Without those protections, however, it risks deepening the very crisis it claims to address. If primary care is truly the foundation of healthcare, then saving it will require not only investment, but rules strong enough to ensure that the needs of patients remain more important than the priorities of shareholders.

– Written by Noah Love, a Content Writer for SPAN.

The 150-Billion Dollar Loophole: Site-Neutral Payments

When a patient comes into a clinic today, the most expensive part of their visit may not be the doctor’s expertise or the technology used for tests; it may be the fee for the facility. Two patients can receive the same course of treatment, but one may go to an independent clinic, while the other may go to a more local clinic that has been bought by a large hospital system. Despite receiving the same treatment, one could be charged up to 60 to 200 percent more simply because of the company. This is the current status of the “site-neutrality payment disparity,” which has sparked a nationwide rebellion in March 2026.

History

Historically, Hospital Outpatient Departments (HOPDs) have received higher reimbursement rates than independent physician offices. The reason being that hospitals carry higher overhead, such as maintaining 24/7 ERs. However, this price gap created a massive incentive for “vertical integration,” or a business strategy where a company controls multiple stages of its supply chain. Systems began aggressively buying up independent practices just to rebrand them as “hospital departments” and trigger those higher fees. As of this year, this trend has left only 30% of U.S. physicians in independent practice, a shift that has stifled competition and sent patient premiums skyrocketing.

Benefits in Primary and Specialty Care

The push for site-neutrality is moving from a policy theory to the clinical setting. On January 1, 2026, new CMS regulations began aligning payments for routine services like drug administration and check-ups across all off-campus settings. The benefits are a major win for the healthcare system in three different ways. First, it offers immediate Patient Justice by lowering out-of-pocket co-pays. Second, it protects Physician Autonomy by removing the financial “bounty” on independent practices, allowing doctors to remain their own bosses. Finally, according to the March 12, 2026, MedPAC Report, expanding these policies to imaging and diagnostics could save the Medicare Trust Fund over $150 billion over the next decade.

Risks and the “Safety Net” Challenge

The path forward demands a balanced perspective, however. The American Hospital Association (AHA) argues in its recent “Healthy Hospitals” campaign that these higher fees actually subsidize essential, money-losing services like burn units and neonatal ICUs. Critics of site-neutrality fear that cutting these payments will force “safety-net” hospitals in rural and underserved areas to shutter critical departments. The ethical challenge for 2026 is ensuring that in the pursuit of efficiency, there won’t be a defunding of the institutions that support communities and beyond.

Conclusion

When a patient walks into a clinic nowadays, the hope is that they will be seen as a person in need of healing, not a source of “facility fee” revenue. The promise of the Site-Neutral Rebellion is not just in lowering a line item on a budget; it is in restoring fairness to the medical marketplace. As healthcare systems continue to evolve, the goals here remain in implementing effective shifts in being able to support patients and hospitals alike. Being able to make a shift towards addressing the gaps between costs for various services and supporting funds in various medical institutions that contribute to patient care services will ensure equitable outcomes for both patients and medical institutions alike.

- Written by Kaulini Chakraborty, Policy Analyst and Content Writer for SPAN

The Hidden Middlemen: How PBMs Shape Drug Prices in America

Why do Americans pay so much for prescription drugs, even when discounts are being negotiated behind the scenes? For many patients, the cost of medications continues to rise despite widespread claims that the system is designed to control prices. While pharmaceutical companies are often blamed for high drug costs, another set of powerful players operates largely out of public view: Pharmacy Benefit Managers, or PBMs. These intermediaries sit between drug manufacturers, insurers, pharmacies, and patients, shaping which medications are covered, how much they cost, and where they can be obtained. As prescription drug spending continues to grow, PBMs have become one of the most influential forces in the U.S. healthcare system. Although PBMs were originally created to lower costs and improve efficiency, their growing market power, opaque pricing practices, and profit-driven incentives have raised serious questions about whether they are fulfilling that mission.

Background

Pharmacy Benefit Managers were initially developed to help insurers manage prescription drug benefits more efficiently. Their core responsibilities include negotiating prices with drug manufacturers, determining which medications are covered through formularies, reimbursing pharmacies, and processing prescription claims. The PBM industry has gone through a large amount of consolidation, where CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group, and Cigna dominate the PBM landscape through their respective subsidiaries. PBMs get revenue by the fees paid to them for their services, as well as a portion of the rebates they negotiate.

This consolidation has given PBMs substantial influence across the entire pharmaceutical supply chain. Because they manage drug benefits for large populations of patients through insurance plans, PBMs have the leverage to negotiate directly with drug manufacturers. In theory, this bargaining power allows them to secure lower prices and pass those savings on to insurers, employers, and patients. However, the complexity of these negotiations and the lack of transparency surrounding them have made it difficult to determine whether these savings are actually reaching consumers.

Support

PBMs can provide great benefits to the healthcare system. PBMs negotiate discounts and rebates from pharmaceutical manufacturers. They also represent a large pool of patients, and PBMs can leverage their scale to push for lower prices than individual insurers or employers could achieve on their own. The negotiating power PBMs hold allows for prices to be decreased system wide.

PBMs also make the jobs of pharmaceutical administration easier, as they centralize the management of prescription drug benefits, process claims, and coordinate pharmacy networks, making it easier for insurers to manage coverage across large populations. Additionally, formularies, lists of covered drugs, can help guide prescribing practices toward more cost-effective options, potentially reducing unnecessary spending.

In today’s healthcare system, PBMs may also play a role in expanding access to care. Their integration with insurers and pharmacies allows for large-scale coordination of drug distribution, and in some cases, they help facilitate access to specialty medications and chronic disease treatments. Given the complexity of modern pharmaceutical care, some level of centralized management may be necessary to ensure that medications are distributed efficiently and consistently.

Criticism

The PBM system has become criticized due to the ability for the middlemen to profit off higher drug prices over lower ones. Rebates and the system behind them has the opportunity to help consumers, as PBMs negotiate rebates from drug manufacturers in exchange for favorable placement on formularies, but rebates are directly linked to a drug’s list price. This creates incentive for PBMs to have higher drug prices, as they can take a portion of the money made off rebates, which increase as drug prices do.

Another major concern is the lack of transparency within the system. Most consumers don’t know PBMs exist, and the fact that they are invisible middlemen leads to misplaced anger on other parts of the system. The Federal Trade Commission has recently expressed concern of PBMs, and they highlight their impact on pricing transparency.

Decreased competition has compounded the criticisms for the PBM system. Companies like CVS Health and UnitedHealth Group own not only PBMs but also insurance plans and pharmacies. A house panel actually found CVS may have broken antitrust laws. This creates potential conflicts of interest, as these corporations may have incentives to steer patients toward their own pharmacy services or prioritize certain medications based on profitability rather than clinical value. The decreased competition in the space also increases how extreme they can prioritize profit margins over consumers.

The impact on independent pharmacies has also been significant. Many smaller pharmacies argue that PBMs reimburse them at unsustainably low rates while imposing additional fees, making it difficult for them to remain in business. This can reduce access to care in certain communities, particularly in rural or underserved areas where independent pharmacies play a critical role.

Patients cannot afford the greediness of these companies, and the PBM system needs overhaul or else customers will be losing a lot more than they gain. In some cases, patients may even pay more for medications through insurance than they would by paying cash, which shows the severity of effects within the system.

Discussion

It is obvious that the PBM system is in need of help, and regulation is the answer. It is important to recognize that PBMs are not the sole drivers of high drug prices. Pharmaceutical manufacturers set initial list prices, and insurers design benefit structures that affect patient costs. PBMs are just the middlemen in the system that are supposed to lower costs, but end up increasing them

With appropriate regulation, PBMs could still fulfill their original purpose of reducing costs and improving access. Increasing transparency is a critical first step. Requiring PBMs to disclose how rebates are negotiated and distributed would allow policymakers and employers to better assess whether savings are reaching patients. Another example of positive reform is a pass through rebate model, where discounts are directly applied to patient costs, which incentivizes lower costs and still earns PBMs profit.

Regulation could also address practices such as spread pricing, where PBMs charge insurers more for a drug than they reimburse pharmacies, keeping the difference as profit. Limiting or eliminating this practice could reduce unnecessary costs within the system. Stronger antitrust enforcement may also be necessary to address the high level of market concentration and prevent further consolidation that could reduce competition.

Regulation however, has been set into motion. In February of 2025, Congress enacted new legislation that aims to control PBMs, such as establishing transparency requirements and allowing for increased oversight over PBMs. Most of these restrictions begin in 2028, and some of the action taken by the FTC has been loopholed by the PBMs. The established regulation is a good start, and long term effects will have to be analyzed before more are put into place. If effective, the regulation could regain the benefits of PBMs while also keeping the incentive for PBMs to keep prices low.

Conclusion

PBMs have one of the most important roles in the U.S healthcare system, defining drug costs for customers. While they were originally designed to reduce costs and improve efficiency, their evolution into powerful potential antitrust violations, lack of clarity in pricing, greedy rebate incentives, and a compounding market has combined to show that PBMs are doing more harm than good.

The debate over rising drug costs often focuses on pharmaceutical companies, but PBMs play an equally important role in determining what patients ultimately pay. The system under which PBMs operate allows for them to continue making a profit over poor practices. Regulation to change that system is the most important way of controlling PBMs, and setting them back on course. The first step is acknowledgement and Congress has begun to work on implementing changes. The American people must stay informed in order to know who is controlling their healthcare.

– Written by Noah Love, a Content Writer for SPAN.

If effective, the regulation could regain the benefits of PBMs while also keeping the incentive for PBMs to keep prices low.

Conclusion

PBMs have one of the most important roles in the U.S healthcare system, defining drug costs for customers. While they were originally designed to reduce costs and improve efficiency, their evolution into powerful potential antitrust violations, lack of clarity in pricing, greedy rebate incentives, and a compounding market has combined to show that PBMs are doing more harm than good.

The debate over rising drug costs often focuses on pharmaceutical companies, but PBMs play an equally important role in determining what patients ultimately pay. The system under which PBMs operate allows for them to continue making a profit over poor practices. Regulation to change that system is the most important way of controlling PBMs, and setting them back on course. The first step is acknowledgement and Congress has begun to work on implementing changes. The American people must stay informed in order to know who is controlling their healthcare.

– Written by Noah Love, a Content Writer for SPAN.
title: The Hidden Middlemen: How PBMs Shape Drug Prices in America

content:
The Telehealth Revolution: Expanding Access or Widening Inequality?

Telehealth has expanded vastly following the COVID-19 pandemic, growing from a reported 25.1% of physicians utilizing telehealth weekly in 2018 to a staggering 71.4% in 2024. Telehealth, which is the provision of healthcare through audio or video calls, websites, and apps, has the potential to connect doctors and patients efficiently and reduce the strain on hospitals without compromising quality of care, but may also come with multiple drawbacks unless properly addressed before the issues become out of hand. Some of these points of contention brought up were that telehealth can widen the digital divide, privacy concerns due to the online platform, and questioned quality of care. This begs the question, how should the limitations of telehealth be addressed to ensure proper care to all?

Access to the technology required to utilize telehealth is not a given for many. Having a proper and stable internet connection can be impossible for some regions to acquire due to the longstanding practice of “digital redlining,” which is increasing internet speeds in areas only where companies have more paying customers. This has drastically favored majority groups and left many regions in a state where residents have no access to internet speeds that could facilitate telehealth, instead being forced to turn to cellular or mobile plans. Furthermore, patients who interface with these digital portals often face further difficulties, as digital literacy and poor audio and video quality often are major barriers. In order to ensure that patients are able to receive an uncompromised quality of care and access to the technology required for telehealth, major development of broadband internet infrastructure is required, as the internet has been identified as one of the most impactful factors when it comes to interfacing with telehealth.

The digital environment has not only brought mechanical issues, but also privacy concerns along with it. Many patients are wary of interacting with telehealth due to the nature of an online service being susceptible to leaking of private information. One of the main causes of this is the physical environment, as many patients are unable to find a space where they can have private conversations with their medical providers in their day-to-day life. Privacy is incredibly important, especially for patients receiving mental health care, or patients who need to share sensitive health information on video. In order to ensure that patients are able to secure a private environment for their telehealth visits, flexibility needs to be integrated into this structure to allow for rescheduling or change of location. Another concern comes from the vulnerabilities that the digital environment allows for. Unsecure networks or phishing links could lure unsuspecting patients into sharing confidential health information or other harmful records that could be used as blackmail, or sold to malicious actors. Procurement of secure connections in a home environment or proper education of individuals about how to identify phishing links or scam websites is required in order to ensure that the privacy of patients is upheld even in a digital environment. Trust is one of the most important factors in healthcare, and maintaining that even in a new virtual space is crucial for patient engagement and willingness to use telehealth.

Telehealth could be a very powerful form of connection and provide accurate diagnosis, however, some occasions may require procedures that would be unavailable on a telehealth visit. One such example emphasized by a study would be comprehensive physical exams for any sort of chest or abdominal pain, and many other issues. These sorts of complications that would require a physical exam are very widespread, and simply verbal discussion may not be enough for a doctor to make a proper diagnosis. This would heavily counteract the accessibility that telehealth could provide, as some patients would need to schedule a follow up after a telehealth check-up, and in that time, potential forgetting of information or handing off a patient could occur, leading to opportunities that could compromise quality of care. However, telehealth visits are not for simply replacing regular examinations, as they could not provide such a thing, but to create an easy way for patients to communicate with doctors and see if their issue could be resolved easier online, or if their complications may require an in-person visit. Telehealth acts as a supplementary way for patients to receive care, and if further procedures are necessary, then they can schedule a later appointment. Proper documentation of telehealth encounters would wade away any sort of confusion surrounding the time delay between visits, and is something that doctors commonly deal with in their day-to-day practices anyway.

Overall, telehealth does come with risks, and the integration of the system requires a larger amount of work to be done in constructing supportive infrastructure, but the supplementary resources that telehealth can provide would be much worth the cost. In order to achieve these widespread efforts to properly integrate telehealth, government regulation would need to come into play to facilitate the growth of the broadband structure, and hospitals would need to create more flexible schedules that allow for patients to find times when they have access to private environments. Education about phishing links and how to identify fraudulent websites would also aid not just telehealth, but also many other sensitive online material that is often used to scam individuals. General digital literacy would be easy to integrate into the education system, and reading material that could help existing adults and especially the elderly become more accustomed to technology would wade away such an issue. Telehealth could be a major step in providing efficiency to our healthcare system, but it requires widespread effort from the public, the government, and the industry to ensure that it can be an effective system.

Written by Nicholas Wright, the editor-in-chief for SPAN.
